title: Shoulder Pain, Droopy Eyelid, Wasted Hand / Look Above the Lung, Not the Shoulder

blocks.text: Shoulder Pain, Droopy Eyelid, Wasted Hand / Look Above the Lung, Not the Shoulder

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-14 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management (published 28 March 2019; last updated March 2024, with minor amendments in February 2026) · Related AMaC: AMaC lobar collapse station; this one tests an apical tumour with nerve involvement
The patient is a man of 63, a retired shipwright. He has had pain in his right shoulder and arm for four months and has noticed his right hand getting weak. Please examine his respiratory system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Shoulder and arm pain, a small droopy eyelid and a wasted hand in a smoker point to a tumour at the top of the lung. The marks come from looking at the face and hand, not just the chest.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates stop at the shoulder and call it a rotator cuff or neck problem, or find nothing in the lungs. Pass: Horner syndrome, hand wasting, apical signs, then lung cancer. Fail: musculoskeletal diagnosis.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Start with the face and hands: look for tar staining, clubbing, a small pupil and a droopy lid.
"May I examine your chest and arms? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; hands, nails, tar staining, face, eyes, neck nodes, trachea.
Examine the chest, then the arm: power, muscle bulk and sensation on the inner side.
"I'm going to feel and listen to your chest, then check the strength and feeling in your arm."
Expansion; percussion; apex; breath sounds; back; nodes; hand muscles; ulnar sensation; reflexes; cover him.
Name the tumour, its effects on the nerves and the tests that decide treatment.
"He has a right apical lung tumour with Horner syndrome and a lower brachial plexus lesion. He needs urgent imaging."
Present in order; diagnosis; why Horner; CT; MRI; PET-CT; MDT; thank him.

Welfare
Starts without consent; moves the painful arm roughly; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, supports the painful arm, and stops if the pain worsens.
R2
A
Systematic technique
Disorganised; omits the eyes, the hand muscles or the apex.
Looks at hands and nails, face and eyes, then neck nodes, trachea, chest front and back, and the arm.
Also tests the supraclavicular fossae, hand grip and sensation over the inner arm.
R3
B
Identifying signs
Reports crackles, a pleural rub or a rash that are not present.
Finds tar staining, a right Horner syndrome, wasting of the small hand muscles, reduced right apical air entry and a dull apex.
Also finds weak finger abduction, reduced sensation over the inner forearm, and a supraclavicular node.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it a rotator cuff injury or cervical spondylosis.
Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour, from lung cancer.
Also names cervical rib, brachial plexus neuritis and apical tuberculosis, and explains why each fits less.
R5
E
Investigations
Asks for a shoulder X-ray only.
Asks for a contrast CT of the chest, liver, adrenals and lower neck, MRI of the superior sulcus, PET-CT and tissue.
Also says CT is done before biopsy, and that a lung cancer multidisciplinary team decides treatment.
R6
E
Pathway and safety
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): attributes it to the neck or shoulder, orders no chest imaging, or discharges him.
Says suspected lung cancer is referred to a lung cancer team, staging comes before treatment, and the pain needs a plan.
Also names induction chemoradiotherapy then surgery for suitable tumours, and smoking cessation support.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: thin; respiratory rate 16; pulse 84 regular; blood pressure 134/80; SpO2 95% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. Tar staining; no clubbing. Right ptosis and a small right pupil; reduced sweating on the right side of the face. Trachea central. Right supraclavicular fossa: a firm node. Right apex: dull percussion and reduced breath sounds. Right hand: wasting of the small muscles and weak finger abduction; reduced sensation over the inner forearm. Left side normal.
Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Explain the Horner syndrome and the hand wasting. (D) 4. Which investigations? (E) 5. How is it treated? (E)

Curveballs: He asks if it could be arthritis: it does not fit. He asks if he will need a biopsy: yes, after staging imaging. He becomes breathless with a swollen face: superior vena cava obstruction, emergency.

Finds Horner syndrome, hand wasting and an apical dull note (B)
Finds tar staining and a supraclavicular node (B)
Names a Pancoast tumour from lung cancer (D)

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): shoulder pain with Horner syndrome and hand wasting in a smoker is a lung tumour. No consent, the chest and eyes skipped, and the cancer missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest and arms? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, face, eyes, neck nodes, trachea; chest front and back; arm power and sensation.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He has tar staining, a right Horner syndrome, hand wasting, a dull right apex and a supraclavicular node. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A Pancoast tumour from lung cancer, with Horner syndrome and a lower brachial plexus lesion. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: Contrast CT of the chest, liver, adrenals and lower neck, MRI of the apex, PET-CT and a biopsy. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Plan?
CANDIDATE: A lung cancer team referral, staging before treatment, and pain control. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not separate other causes, or name the treatment pathway.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll support your arm and stop if it hurts. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, nails, face, eyes, nodes, trachea; chest; supraclavicular fossae; grip, abduction, inner forearm sensation.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Right Horner syndrome, wasted hand muscles, weak abduction, reduced inner forearm sensation, dull apex, node, tar staining. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A Pancoast tumour. A cervical rib, brachial neuritis and apical tuberculosis fit less, because of Horner syndrome and the node. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: Contrast CT of the chest, liver, adrenals and lower neck before biopsy; MRI of the superior sulcus; PET-CT; tissue. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Plan?
CANDIDATE: Lung cancer team discussion; induction chemoradiotherapy then surgery if suitable; smoking cessation support. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, the nodes and sensation, the differential, CT before biopsy, MRI of the sulcus, PET-CT and the treatment pathway.
R2: Looking only at the shoulder. The eyes, hands and nodes carry the diagnosis.
R4: Calling it musculoskeletal. Shoulder pain with Horner syndrome and hand wasting in a smoker is a lung apex tumour.
R5: Asking for a shoulder X-ray. The tumour needs CT and MRI, and staging decides treatment.
R6: Discharging with physiotherapy. A delay in the cancer pathway harms him.
"Let me look at his eyes and hand again before I go on."
"He has Horner syndrome and hand wasting, so I'd say a Pancoast tumour."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Pancoast syndrome: shoulder pain spreading down the inner arm, Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from the stellate ganglion, and wasting of the small hand muscles from the lower brachial plexus.

NICE NG122: contrast CT of the chest, liver, adrenals and lower neck before any biopsy (1.2.2, 1.2.14); PET-CT for people who could have curative treatment (1.2.4); MRI for superior sulcus tumours when necessary (1.2.7); refer to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team.
Treatment for suitable tumours: induction concurrent chemoradiotherapy then surgery (SWOG S9416, Rusch et al, J Clin Oncol 2007); the lung cancer multidisciplinary team decides.
THINK: Shoulder pain, Horner, wasted hand: Pancoast.
SAY: "A tumour at the top of the lung, pressing on nerves."
DO: Look at the eyes; check inner forearm sensation.
NUMBERS: CT before biopsy; MRI for superior sulcus (NG122).
TRAP: Rotator cuff; discharge.
FINISH: CT, MRI, PET-CT, tissue, lung cancer team.
